AgVita: no detectable nitrate and high molybdenum. NovaCrop: reasonable nitrate, lower moly. Copper reads satisfactory on AgVita but low on both leaves on NovaCrop, and a third the value in the young leaf. Boron similar — Jimmy doesn’t accept AgVita’s optimal range there. Jamie’s approach, offered up deliberately to be challenged: ignore the ammonium and nitrate split and go to total nitrogen — the actual energy outcome in the plant. Young leaf sitting well ahead of old leaf signals an oncoming deficiency regardless of what the other forms are doing, and there aren’t large reserves in the others on a parts basis. The same differential argues an oncoming phosphorus deficiency too, with phosphorus applied as straight MAP at 80 kg/ha.

mtg-notes-0807.title: AI, and what cuts through it

items.text: Shared a marketing email from a company whose material he normally finds genuinely useful, and this one told him nothing he wanted to know about the product. The tells: repeated words nobody actually says, and sentences that lecture rather than lead — someone else added the dashes, “every time I see dashes, I know it’s AI.” First time their email read like something he could have got out of ChatGPT himself.

What cuts through the noise is a customer reading an email and knowing Hamilton wrote it. AI is a powerful tool and it is not going away, but there is a widening window for things that feel human — at a marketing and a sales level — and everyone leaning on the machine falls by the wayside in it. Where you have the time, form your own thoughts and write your own emails.

Nothing sciency about it — footage of sampling and running the tools — and growers who knew nothing about silica now feel like they do, and want some.

items.lead: Heavy metals — wider than we thought
items.text: The agreement covers the whole range for heavy metal testing, not just the one product that raised the issue. That was understood as product-specific along the chain and wasn’t — Jamie and Amos both put their hand up for it. Away now: Aminoplex (result already back, sent July), FKF, K-Max, OptiCal and PowerCal, and OptiTrace boron, copper, iron, manganese, moly and zinc. Amos is reconciling the rest against the full organic list and sending the gaps. Turnaround is 7–10 business days. If an order is held awaiting a heavy metals test, that is why.

Testing is per batch, so a new batch needs a new test. Nate should forecast organic traces into the system even where orders aren’t firm, so stock-take shows a batch running low early enough to get testing underway. BudMax and OptiTrace Max are going forward now for the organic growers coming into spring. It is an ongoing requirement, though a run of clean results makes it a fair conversation at the next audit.

Montague hold about 18 shuttles of calcium chloride bought through a tender, and want it gone rather than carried into next year. They don’t have to use all of it. Their preference was the apples, to maximise calcium; cherries were raised and steered away from. They are not replacing PowerCal — this is on top.

Chelsea inferred it was in the system before anyone told her: leaf chloride was significantly high last year with no matching soil chloride. She asked point blank whether they were spraying calcium chloride and was told no — which was probably honest, because the label reads Cal 175 and, as Hamilton put it, growers often have no idea what form they are using. That sent everyone down a rabbit hole of water quality and Humix at the rhizosphere. Colour in their Pinks is their biggest hindrance, and excess chloride does much the same thing as nitrogen applied too late.

Cal 175 is 17.5% calcium and 31% chloride. Ten foliar applications at 10 L/ha puts about 31 units of chloride straight onto the leaf, against a soil test that might total something similar. For a highly mobile nutrient Hamilton called that a no-go zone.

Fertigate it, don’t spray it — in with the OptiCal fertigation at late flower, the same trick already used to carry leftover thiocal and thio-K in on an existing application rather than adding a pass. 50 L/ha, potentially up to 100. Fertigated, the chloride displaces through the soil instead of sitting on leaf and fruit; it disassociates almost immediately and about 75 mm of rain moves the lot, which is why soil tests before and after rain read so differently. The young trees are the better home for it than the mature blocks — 18 ha, already on a fortnightly fertigation, growth lost last year to make up, and chloride is a vegetative nutrient. The seven hectares of pears won’t make a dent. Leaf tests through the season, and cut it the moment chloride climbs.

If the product weren’t already sitting on the farm with a requirement to use it up, nobody here would put it in the program. It isn’t that it is bad — it is a lot of calcium, cheap, and reasonably cost-effective fertigated — it is that the program doesn’t need it. Tuesday’s session with Montague partly exists so their team knows where not to use it; some have already gone rogue with PowerCal and OptiTrace boron, which are better things to go rogue with.

items.text: Jimmy compared sap results showing boron uptake after early applications but calcium still appearing low. The team cautioned against treating a generic calcium target range as a crop-stage target. Once the soil test was opened, pH around 8 and high potassium became the main leads to investigate, alongside the young-versus-old-leaf pattern. Having calcium in the soil does not establish that it is available to the plant.

A barley sap test had about 10.9 ppm boron in the young leaf, strong calcium and phosphorus, and a crop that still looked healthy. Jimmy suspected roots had reached an alkaline subsoil layer as manganese fell in the new leaf. The discussion compared an apple result around 30 ppm without visible symptoms with Woody’s citrus results around 120–150 ppm, where flowering and tree performance were poor. These were observations from different crops, not agreed toxicity thresholds or application targets. Woody suspects boron below the usual 15 cm soil-sampling depth and has taken fresh leaf samples to check.

An external analysis initially appeared well below the blend supplied. Working through the actual report with Smithy, Josh, Jamie and Hamilton showed a calculation and interpretation issue. Check the laboratory report, bag analysis and quoted units together. A weight-by-weight percentage cannot be compared directly with a weight-by-volume percentage without the product’s density; partial-area spreading also changes the units per treated hectare. Hamilton used a 60% spread area as an example of why a whole-hectare calculation can disagree with the quote.

Tom described previous results that needed retesting because the laboratory had used soil-test calibration for a fertiliser sample. Small grab samples from a large dry blend can also skew individual nutrients, as happened with variations between Handpicked blends. Sample handling matters too: an AdBlue sample taken in an old soft-drink bottle had been contaminated by the container. Ingredient quantities, batch records and total blend weights provide the internal checks to compare against.

Jamie asked the team to respond calmly, get the report and work through the calculation and testing method before accepting that the product is wrong. Chelsea will follow up any further reports and suggested keeping this worked example in Odoo Knowledge so the team can refer to it next time.

gsbNotes.text: Four microbes selected as the highest organic-acid producers GSB could screen. They release phosphorus that is locked up — to calcium in high-pH soils, to iron and aluminium in low-pH — with gluconic acid doing most of the work and citric acid secondary. Only 20–30% of applied P is ever taken up; the rest fixes. Chemistry can break those bonds too, but it re-locks within a week, whereas the microbes keep doing it as long as they survive. Grant frames it as a soil conditioner, and was clear it is not the same job as Lockout.

The bigger idea underneath it, from Kamal: when phosphate is liberated, nitrogen availability rises with it — DNA synthesis needs phosphorus, and without it the plant can’t properly access nitrogen or the micronutrients either. That reframes SP from a phosphorus product into a nitrogen-efficiency product.

In the furrow. Liquid inject is the Rolls-Royce — and the reason matters: even where seed-applied fungicide kills a patch, you get re-inoculation once the fungicide dissipates. Seed coating loses on real estate rather than biology, because everything wants to be on the seed and there is usually a fungicide already there. A coated compost granule holds spores beautifully but costs the grower more. Ground spray is last and least targeted.

gsbNotes.lead: The only field result on SP
gsbNotes.text: A yield bump in canola on GSB’s local ground where phosphorus was locked up by aluminium. That is the whole evidence base Grant offered — unquantified, one site, one crop, no replication described, and nobody asked. Worth recording as exactly that.

Deliberately fungal-biased: three fungi plus an actinomycete, because in our farming systems the bacteria survive and the fungi don’t. Enzymatic breakdown of cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin and pectin — canola being the hard one on lignin. Take just 1% of the carbon out of that matter and the cementing holding the cell wall together fails, so it degrades fast. It colonises internally and works from the inside out, which Jimmy had seen in a trial near Albury.

gsbNotes.lead: And it competes for the substrate
gsbNotes.text: The same organisms consume the carbon and nitrogen that stubble-borne pathogens rely on, so there is less for them to carry into the next crop. GSB’s trial work used cereal stubble and compared treated against untreated and against a nutrition-only product. Grant’s competitive point: products that rely on enzymes or nutrition plus whatever biology is already in the paddock risk proliferating the resident pathogens along with everything else — his words were that they run a very real risk, not that it always happens.

Base recommendation is DigestMate onto stubble with about 8 kg/ha of ammonium sulfate. Be clear why: ammonium sulfate wins on economics, not biology. Urea works too and is slightly more complex for the microbes; amino acid and protein sources are fine; fish hydrolysate may be better again because the nitrogen is directly available. Nitrate is ruled out. Whether it is the ammonium or the sulfur doing the work was asked directly and never answered, so we can’t make a sulfur claim.

gsbNotes.lead: Rain, and how long it will wait
gsbNotes.text: It needs rain to be at its best but will sit on stubble from early summer after harvest and survive until it comes, within reason. Three months of 45°C will kill it. Apply any time after harvest.

It starts at the base of the stubble because that is where the residual moisture sits, so the field check is whether the stubble pulls out easily at the base. It will not look dramatic from the ute. The lab check is a C:N ratio before and after against an untreated control — a carbon reduction means it is working. Evidence to date is mostly South Australian cropping-belt grower feedback rather than replicated trials.

Three microbes on an endophytic Trichoderma backbone, all chosen as very rapid growers. They colonise the rhizosphere and phytosphere, out-populate anything pathogenic, steal its breakfast and then act as a bouncer on the door. Good results on high-Fusarium Queensland soils; currently being trialled in cotton on Verticillium. Grant was upfront: “by no means 100% effective 100% of the time — that’s not the world we live in in this biological space.”

gsbNotes.lead: Lockout is carbon-led, DigestMate is nitrogen-led
gsbNotes.text: Jamie asked whether Lockout’s food source follows the same principles. Grant started with “nitrogen, carbon” then corrected himself in the room and settled on more so carbon in that circumstance. A clean contrast between two products that otherwise sound like they want the same thing.

gsbNotes.lead: Lockout in orchards goes on at budswell
gsbNotes.text: Through budswell and certainly before flowering, to get colonisation established in the ground ahead of the pathogen becoming active. Grant, on the orchard he visited with Chelsea and Andrew where there is significant vascular disease. Lab reports are still pending, so his pathogen identification is a working assumption. This is the substance of the email he owes Chelsea.

gsbNotes.lead: Soil temperature — the fungi start at 5°C
gsbNotes.text: Bruce asked whether anything actually happens in the top 10 cm below 8°C. Kamal: the fungal side proliferates from 5°C, works across 5–30°C with an optimum around 25°C, but bacteria stall below about 15°C. Multiplication at 5–6°C is real, just slower. That is the honest answer to “it’s too cold for biology” on a winter-sown furrow — and a genuine point of difference against a bacterial-only inoculant. One to put back to GSB: the organism that differentiates SP is a bacterium, so cold-soil furrow work leans on the fungal fraction.

gsbNotes.lead: We are outnumbered about a thousand to one
gsbNotes.text: Kamal’s own arithmetic, and the most useful number in the meeting. We apply somewhere around 1–3 million cells; resident soil populations are around a billion per gram, and a heavy Fusarium load is a billion per gram on its own. That is why the food source isn’t optional, why proliferation rather than the applied dose does the work, and why a simple sugar feeds the wrong side. It also honestly qualifies the out-populate story above.

Grant flagged it unprompted: he does not use kill, suppress or control. The word is balance. Partly APVMA exposure, partly because it is the accurate description — nothing is being killed, it is being consumed, which leaves less opportunity for pathogens to proliferate. Worth adopting across our copy, and worth noting it rules out any claim framed as a reduction in disease incidence.

GSB has removed molasses as a food source entirely, and the same goes for glucose, sucrose and fructose. Simple sugars feed the resident pathogen load faster than they feed what we apply — see the thousand-to-one above. Use complex carbon instead: humic, fulvic, fish, seaweed. Kamal’s framing — molasses is fast food, humic is a meal you have to cook. One exception: where a test shows beneficials already outnumber pathogens, molasses is fine to push proliferation.

gsbNotes.lead: Nitrogen nutrition decides who you feed
gsbNotes.text: Jimmy put it up and Kamal confirmed it: feed a crop hard on nitrogen, accumulate nitrates, and the plant exudes free amino acids and simple sugars rather than complex ones — which is food for the pathogens rather than for the Trichoderma. It is the causal chain that connects a nutrition decision to a root-disease outcome without making a disease claim, and it explains why intensively fed horticulture gets root disease.

gsbNotes.lead: Carbon sets the recommendation, not soil type
gsbNotes.text: Asked which soil types suit, Kamal declined the texture framing entirely: it depends on carbon. Under 2% soil carbon, add a humic starter with the biology so it can fire up. Above 2%, he is not recommending humic or sugar at all. The best combination he named: a carbon source, a nitrogen source like fish, and a seaweed extract.

gsbNotes.lead: Carbon building is a five-to-ten-year play
gsbNotes.text: Fungal necromass is the stable form — melanin is very stable in soil. Kamal: visible at about five years, ten to judge it properly, and the fungal-to-bacterial rebalance sits on the same horizon. A strong year-one solubilisation response followed by tillage is a warning rather than a win, because year two it is gone. The room did not land on no-till dogma though: compacted ground needs oxygen for the fungi, and strategic tillage can sit alongside microbial application.

gsbNotes.lead: Liquid for foliar, powder for soil
gsbNotes.text: The liquid is roughly 80% metabolites and 20% spores. The metabolites do two jobs: inhibit pathogen growth, and signal the plant to switch on its own systemic resistance. That is why liquid beats powder as a foliar. Powder is mostly spores, which attach to carbon quickly and get through the rhizosphere — better for a root pathogen. And a granule and a powder are not the same thing.

A field rule that has nothing to do with GSB’s products and is immediately usable: never apply calcium when the stomata are shut — at night, or under scorching midday heat. Calcium moves on the transpiration stream, so apply when transpiration is running. The tell that it went on at the wrong time is calcium sitting in the leaf test while the fruit stays deficient, especially in citrus. This constrains our own standing Lockout mix, which carries PowerCal.

gsbNotes.lead: Calcium can re-fix what SP just released
gsbNotes.text: Kamal flagged the interaction: where you have plenty of phosphate-solubilising bacteria working, applied calcium can re-fix the phosphorus they just released, and pH wants to sit around seven. Whether he meant soil pH or tank pH wasn’t made clear — worth confirming before we put a number on it. Our standing cereal recipe pairs Lockout with humic and PowerCal, and the “is there anything else worth adding” question never got answered.

Never leave mixed product in a tank overnight. The spores go vegetative, block the sprayer, and die under pressure in that form. Spray pressure itself is not the problem — it is pressure over time, and a spray system only exposes them momentarily, so 15 bar in passing is fine. That is field experience rather than tested data. There is no EC or tank-concentration threshold — GSB has not trialled it and would not nominate a number.

Compatibility work exists for Trichoderma with a handful of registered fungicides and with glyphosate, but Grant framed that as a concession to grower nervousness rather than best practice — best practice is that the fungicide isn’t there and the pathogens are out-populated instead. His broader position on fungicide overuse driving resistant Fusarium, Verticillium and black root rot is strongly held; paraphrase it, don’t quote it. No compatibility statement was given for DigestMate with copper, despite the question naming copper.

Worth having straight for potato, cherry, avocado and tree-crop conversations. Phytophthora is an oomycete, not a true fungus, which is part of why fungicides have had a hard time with it — and it is picking up resistance to most of them. Its spores carry a flagellum and swim: a film of water, mist, fog or irrigation water and it moves through a block overnight. GSB’s answer is competition rather than control.

GSB’s metagenomic soil test reports carbon, the fungal-to-bacterial ratio, and counts of both pathogens and beneficials. Around 1 fungi to 50 bacteria is fine in high-nitrogen annuals like wheat, 1:20 is the aspiration, and worse than 1:100 is a problem. Horticulture wants fungal dominance — and GSB has never yet measured a fungal-dominant soil in their testing. It matters commercially: bacteria-dominant, the plant keeps only 20–30% of its photosynthate; balanced, it keeps 50–60%.

gsbNotes.lead: Compost teas — the objection is risk, not efficacy
gsbNotes.text: Grant conceded plainly that growers do get an effect and that increasing microbial diversity is a good thing they support. The objection is that on-farm brewing carries an unmanaged contamination risk, including a genuine health risk to anyone immunocompromised, and that the cost per microbe is poor against a manufactured product. If compost is used it needs to hit 70°C at the thermophilic stage and then humify — end up like a humic substance, not like compost — and every batch should be tested.

Kamal has run our FKF in the lab as a food source: Trichoderma proliferation was so high it filled a plate overnight, against the usual two days and two nights. He has already started recommending it to GSB’s own testers. One caveat — he suspects a preservative in it that suppresses the bacterial side; we need to confirm whether there is one. And a caution we raised ourselves: something that wins on a plate can still lose in the paddock if it is a simple sugar.

gsbNotes.lead: We still have no application rate
gsbNotes.text: The single biggest gap. Across the whole session the only rate given was the 8 kg/ha ammonium sulfate food source. Nothing on product rate, water rate, nozzle, filter, tank-mix order, jar test, seed-coat loading, granule blend rate, liquid or powder shelf life, or storage temperature. The granule figure of six months is borrowed off GSB’s rhizobium granules; they expect to beat it because these organisms are spore-formed, and Grant will review it in a few months. Registration status was never mentioned. First follow-up.

Grant is writing an agronomist’s summary covering all three products and where each best fits, and has already posted a paper on selecting microbial products by formulation type to the shared WhatsApp group — several of the team still need adding to it. We are to send food-source samples for plate testing, as single products and as mixtures, at recommended dose and at 1% and 2%. Andrew to supply the macadamia flower pathogen names and send diseased samples. Grant owes Chelsea the orchard email once the lab reports land. Next catch-up to be booked sooner than the last gap.

Whether DigestMate can be used in-crop, mid-season for disease protection was asked twice and drifted both times — no in-crop use is endorsed, and nobody should infer one. And horticultural leaf digestion has no trial data at all; Andrew is only just starting on nut trees, so any horticulture position is mechanism and theory only.
